title: The genius of corvids
text: Crows and ravens were long dismissed as vermin, and the {{1}} (DESCRIBE) suited farmers who lost crops to them every season. Science has since revised that judgement completely. In laboratory tests, corvids solve puzzles that defeat many mammals: New Caledonian crows bend twigs into hooks, and when a first attempt proves {{2}} (EFFECT), they discard it and start again. In the wild, they hide food while keeping track of exactly who was watching them — behaviour that implies a {{3}} (AWARE) of other minds once thought uniquely human. Ravens also play for the sheer {{4}} (ENJOY) of it, tobogganing down snowy rooftops, and they hold grudges: in one famous study, crows scolded the researchers who had trapped them for years afterwards, and even their uninvolved {{5}} (COLLEAGUE) joined in. All this {{6}} (INTELLIGENT) is expensive to run, which may explain why corvids have unusually large brains for their size and a notably long {{7}} (ADOLESCENT), spent learning from experienced adults. Whatever the mechanism, the old caricature of the bird that fears a stuffed shirt on a pole now looks thoroughly {{8}} (DATE).

gaps.explanation: 'the description suited farmers' — noun from describe.
'a first attempt proves ineffective' — negative prefix in-.
'implies an awareness of other minds' — noun from aware.
'the sheer enjoyment of it' — noun from enjoy.
'their uninvolved colleagues joined in' — plural noun.
'a notably long adolescence' — noun from adolescent.
'now looks thoroughly outdated' — out- + date, no longer fashionable.
